edges.reason: Maps how a gaseous flame sits in the CIR, which is context for material tests but not a flammability limit for cabin fabrics.
Inverse flames change where the oxygen is, a useful bound when habitat oxygen is enriched, but the fuel is ethylene gas.
Not a spacesuit-atmosphere materials test. Oxygen in these runs is a flame-structure variable.
Fundamental gaseous-flame structure, weak link to terrestrial firefighting gear.
Still-atmosphere flammability is the no-ventilation limit inside a rack or a closed volume on station.
Oxygen was varied from about 21 percent up through the mid-30s and 40 percent, the range expected in a lunar habitat.
The high-oxygen BRE points are the closest still-air screen to a suit atmosphere short of the CFI-G burner.
A method for screening materials without a large fire, not a detector or turnout-gear result.
Shows how a laminar jet flame behaves without buoyancy. Indirect for cabin material selection.
Coflow speed is a stand-in for ventilation, but the fuel is gas, not habitat plastic or fabric.
Does not address 100 percent oxygen at suit pressure.
Laboratory flame structure, not firefighter equipment.
A gaseous-flame body-force study. Secondary to BASS and SAME for station operations.
The Moon is partial gravity. Until LUCI and FM2 fly, E-FIELD is the PSI stand-in that puts a force on the flame.
Does not reproduce suit oxygen concentration.
Ion-driven flow is a research tool, not a fire-service product.
Explains why a station flame is spherical and diffusion-limited once buoyancy is gone.
Spherical flames are the zero-g end of the bound. Lunar gravity sits between this and a normal flame.
Shape study, not a suit-material limit.
The contrast with a teardrop flame is teaching material, not a product.
Directly the materials and the low-speed ventilation a crew cabin actually has.
Solid fuels (films, fabrics) plus a measured oxygen level are what a lunar habitat material screen needs.
Shows how the same solids behave as oxygen rises, which is the direction a suit prebreathe and cabin move.
Suppression and spread on thin materials informs how fabrics burn, loosely related to turnout gear.
SIBAL fabric and PMMA in the glovebox duct, plus a nitrogen-style extinguisher already used on station.
Thicker, realistic solids in a forced flow. Habitat oxygen will be higher than these early runs, so read them as the low-oxygen bound.
Useful geometry (fire behind an object, wake flames) but not 100 percent oxygen.
Extinguisher effectiveness on small solids. The flight hardware is not a ground extinguisher.
Droplet fuels in cabin atmospheres. Cool-flame survival means a visible extinction is not always the end of combustion.
Oxygen and diluent were varied. Cool flames are a suppression false-negative, not a materials limit.
Droplet chemistry, not suit fabric.
Explains reignition after an apparent extinguishment. Indirect for terrestrial nozzles.
Nuisance dust on station is why a smoke detector false-alarms. DAFT measures that background.
Lunar dust is the same problem, sharper. A detector that cannot tell dust from smoke will alarm whenever the habitat is dirty.
Not a suit-fire experiment.
This is the flight root of the shuttle detector that separates smoke from dust, later used in mines.
Soot-point models support how much smoke a detector might see. Secondary to SAME itself.
No habitat oxygen or dust measurement.
No suit condition.
Soot modeling only.
A way to extrapolate BASS spread instead of burning every material on station.
The model is only as good as the BASS oxygen range it was checked against.
Not validated at suit oxygen.
Numerical method, not hardware.
Extinction of droplet flames when oxygen, pressure, and a slow flow change. That is the suppression corner of station fire safety.
Oxygen mole fractions in the test matrix reach about 0.30, which touches the lunar-habitat band.
Droplets, not a suit liner.
Helium and nitrogen dilution is the same idea as inerting a compartment.
The suppression dataset: carbon dioxide and helium dilution, with oxygen mole fraction and droplet size for hundreds of burns.
Most runs sit near Earth oxygen. Use it for the suppressant, not for a 30 percent oxygen material limit.
Does not cover a pure-oxygen suit.
Fine water mist for the ISS came from this suppression line of work and is used on the ground. Dilution limits travel the same way.
The first burn bigger than an index card in a real spacecraft volume, at cabin oxygen near 21 percent and a set airflow.
Scale is right for a habitat. Oxygen in Saffire-I is still the station value, so it is the low-oxygen large-fire bound.
Too big and too lean to be a suit fire. It bounds the vehicle the suit returns to.
Large-sample spread in a confined volume is a research result, not a ground product.
The material menu for a cabin: silicone, Nomex, PMMA, SIBAL, at about 20 cm/s and about 21 percent oxygen.
Same solids a habitat will fly. Oxygen is still near 21 percent, so treat spread rates as a lower bound.
Nomex and silicone are suit-adjacent materials, but the test atmosphere is not 100 percent oxygen at 4.3 psi.
Nomex and silicone results are the closest flight data to protective clothing.
Raises the airflow on a meter-scale sample. Ventilation is what feeds a station fire once buoyancy is gone.
Flow comparison at large scale. Oxygen is still the station mix.
Vehicle-scale, not suit-scale.
Confined-flow spread, indirect.
The detector design input: droplet size and how fast smoke moves when there is no buoyant plume.
Particle sizes still apply. Dust interference is DAFT, not SAME-R.
No suit-volume smoke test.
Low-gravity particle sizes explain why a spacecraft detector is built differently from a ceiling alarm.
Primary detection dataset. Smoke in microgravity does not rise, so particle size and the forced flow set the alarm.
The materials are spacecraft materials. Pair it with DAFT before trusting an alarm in dust.
Does not size smoke inside a suit.
The shuttle detector that ignores dust grew out of this smoke-versus-nuisance work, including mining use.
Liftoff and flame structure in the glovebox duct. Background for BASS, not the material limit.
No enriched-oxygen solid sample.
Not applicable.
Not a product path.
Soot onset changes what a smoke detector sees. Secondary to SAME's particle sizes.
No lunar-oxygen materials matrix.
Not a suit test.
Smoke-point data is a combustion metric, weakly tied to alarms.
Included because it is combustion-adjacent fluid physics in the archive. It does not set a flammability limit.
No oxygen or material flammability result.
No suit result.
No fire-service result.
Turns SAME particle data into a smoke field a detector designer can place a sensor in.
The model inherits SAME's materials and flows, not a lunar dust case.
Not a suit volume.
Smoke-transport modeling is how a less-nuisance detector gets its thresholds.
Cool-flame extinction diameter is a suppression limit for small droplets after FLEX.
Pressure and fuel studies. Not a habitat material.
Not suit-scale.
Extinction-diameter correlations are research results.
Stretch and radiation extinction bound when a cool flame dies. Secondary to FLEX.
No habitat oxygen series in the table we hold.
Not applicable.
Counterflow extinction is a lab method.
Most station air is 21 percent oxygen. CFI-G is the enriched-oxygen extreme, not the daily cabin.
A lunar habitat is expected at 30 percent oxygen or more, at 10.2 psi or less. CFI-G is the only PSI series that reaches well above that, up to about 85 percent.
A suit is 100 percent oxygen at 4.3 psi. CFI-G does not hit 4.3 psi, but it is the high-oxygen flame data that bounds suit fire behavior.
High-oxygen burner flames are not a ground fire-service dataset.
